<paper id="2609.28900v2"><page num="1">CODETTA: High-Capacity, Keyless, and Undetectable
Multi-Agent Collusion
Qi Pang Virginia Smith Wenting Zheng
Carnegie Mellon University
{qipang, smithv, wenting}@cmu.edu
Abstract
Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in high-
stakes settings such as finance, healthcare, and software engineering, where agents coordinate through
natural-language messages. These same communication channels, however, can also enable colluding
agents to exfiltrate confidential information or coordinate unauthorized actions. Steganography makes
such behavior particularly difficult to detect by hiding covert communication within outputs that appear
ordinary to an auditor reading the transcript.
Existing provably undetectable LLM steganography protocols, however, are not suited to realistic de-
ployments. High-capacity schemes typically assume a symmetric setting where the receiver can reproduce
the sender’s output distribution. The state-of-the-art practical protocol for asymmetric agents has very low
capacity. Additionally, most existing approaches rely on a pre-shared secret key.
In this paper, we make the systematic threat of undetectable agent collusion concrete by proposing
CODETTA, a high-capacity steganographic protocol for independently deployed agents under realistic
asymmetric settings. CODETTA combines a shared public model for estimating the communication
channel, a sampling mechanism that preserves the sender’s output distribution, and an adaptive error-
correcting code for high-capacity communication. It further removes the need for a pre-shared secret key
through a steganographic key-exchange protocol, enabling independently deployed agents to establish a
shared key while keeping their communication transcript computationally indistinguishable from ordinary
model outputs.
Across three agent workloads and three sender models, CODETTA achieves up to 94× the capacity of
the state-of-the-art asymmetric protocol. Its key exchange establishes a shared key using approximately
80k visible tokens, with an empirically certified failure probability of at most 4.1 × 10
−3 
across all
three workloads. These results show that effectively undetectable collusion is becoming feasible even
between independently deployed agents, and we suggest that auditing mechanisms must be amended with
complementary techniques beyond simply inspecting agents’ communication transcripts.
1 Introduction
Multi-agent systems powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in high-
stakes workflows across finance, healthcare, and software engineering [GCW
+
24,XSLW25,TZZ
+

+
24,

+
24]. In these systems, autonomous agents are designed to communicate, coordinate, and delegate sub-
tasks, often via natural language messages. However, the same communication channel also enables collusion
among agents. Agents often have access to sensitive information that they are not allowed to disclose under
organizational or regulatory policies, and compromised or misaligned agents may pursue objectives that are
not authorized by their operators. In either case, the agents can use their communication channel to leak
confidential information or to coordinate unauthorized actions.
Such collusion is no longer hypothetical, and can even emerge on its own in agentic systems. For example,
in July 2026, OpenAI reported that 1,200 autonomous agents that were running during internal evaluations
1
arXiv:2609.28900v2 [cs.CR] 25 Sep 2026</page><page num="3">open key exchange over the channel, such as Diffie–Hellman, reveals to the auditor that secret messages
are being transmitted. So the paradox is that the agents need a covert channel to establish the key and a key
to construct the covert channel. A recent theoretical work proposes a steganographic key exchange that
tolerates noisy channels [VZ26] to address this challenge. Their feedback compiler transmits the exchange
bit by bit, signaling every bit over a fixed number of token blocks, and its alternative construction avoids
this bitwise signaling under sparse-secret LPN with quasi-polynomial security. Under practical constraints,
our estimate in Section 7.4 gives about 2 million published tokens for a single 128-bit key exchange, and
the construction has not been evaluated in practical agent systems.
These limitations leave open the central question of this work:
Can independently deployed, asymmetric LLM agents bootstrap a shared secret from scratch and collude at
high capacity over monitored channels without being detected?
1.1 Contributions
We answer this question with CODETTA, a high-capacity, keyless, and provably undetectable steganographic
collusion framework for multi-agent systems. Two independently hosted agents establish a shared key over
the audited channel and then transmit high-capacity payloads, and we prove that the resulting transcripts are
computationally indistinguishable from ordinary agent outputs. Our contributions are as follows.
• High-capacity asymmetric steganography. CODETTA introduces a small public draft model that both
agents run on the public transcript as a shared reference distribution; without it, the receiver would decode
every token with the same fixed alphabet and error rate and waste the entropy of the text. At each step,
the draft model partitions the vocabulary into buckets and decides how many payload bits the step can
carry, and a maximal-coupling construction samples the published token exactly from the sender’s private
distribution, so that the disagreement between the two distributions becomes a substitution channel. We
design an alphabet-adaptive error-correcting code to match the alphabet size to the entropy of each token,
and the receiver decodes the payload with belief propagation.
• Efficient keyless steganographic key exchange. CODETTA bootstraps its shared secret by transporting
MLWE ciphertexts over a keyless steganographic carrier: every published block is an honest sample
from the sender’s model, and each ciphertext coefficient becomes a small displacement that the lattice
construction absorbs as additional noise. The protocol relies on the MLWE assumptions as in ML-KEM-
512 and, to our knowledge, is the first implemented steganographic key exchange between independently
deployed LLM agents. CODETTA carries a full q-ary coefficient per block and corrects the carrier’s
errors once, so a 128-bit key exchange publishes about 80k tokens, about 23× fewer than our estimate in
Section 7.4 for the construction of [VZ26].
• 
Evaluation. We evaluate CODETTA on three realistic agent workloads and three widely used sender LLMs.
CODETTA achieves up to 94× the capacity of the asymmetric protocol of [BYP
+

every transmitted message and preserving the model output distribution, and the key exchange establishes

These results show that effectively undetectable collusion is becoming feasible even between indepen-
dently deployed agents, suggesting that defenses should move beyond transcript inspection toward comple-
mentary strategies, including auditing agents’ actions to identify suspicious coordination, and perturbing the
communication channel to reduce or disrupt the capacity for covert communication (see Section 9).
3</page><page num="6">that operates a consulting agent to provide market analysis to institutional clients, and an asset management
fund whose execution agent continuously queries the consulting agent for automated portfolio rebalancing.
The bank may possess material non-public information, such as unannounced mergers, impending regulatory
sanctions, or unreleased earnings, while the fund may hold private information about its clients’ accounts and
positions. The two parties may therefore benefit from exchanging information that neither is permitted to
disclose, and the compliance teams of both organizations audit the messages between the two agents. If the
agents can encode the name of an impending merger or a confidential client position inside normal messages,
the auditor observes benign text while the prohibited information crosses the organizational boundary.
In both scenarios, the auditor wants to detect the misaligned behavior and the insider trading from the
messages that the agents exchange, and the rest of this section defines the setting and the auditor precisely.
3.2 Setting
CODETTA works in multi-agent setting, but for simplicity, we focus on analyzing two agents, namely a sender
and a receiver. They exchange natural language messages over a communication channel that an independent
auditor audits for misbehavior. The communication channel can be any channel that the agents can read from
and write their outputs to, including the communication messages and the shared file systems or even the
editable public wiki as mentioned in Section 1. The agents generate every message token by token using its
own language model, and all the outputs of both agents form the public transcript.

The sender wants to deliver a message m to the receiver inside its ordinary responses. The receiver
must recover m from the published tokens alone, and the transcript must remain indistinguishable from the
transcript of ordinary responses as in Definition 2 (see Section 3.4). We first present a keyed regime, in
which the two agents are assumed to share a secret key. We later remove this assumption by designing a
steganographic key exchange protocol.
3.3 Threat model
The adversaries are the two colluding agents. They aim to communicate secret messages through LLM output
channels without being detected. They may run different models, but both follow the steganographic protocol
6</page><page num="7">and want to exchange a payload that policy forbids, such as sensitive data or a colluding signal. Each agent
controls only its own generation. In the keyed regime the two agents share a secret key, and in the keyless
regime they share nothing beyond the public protocol, whose parameters carry no secret and can be fixed by
the protocol specification.
The auditor is the defender. We consider a passive but strong auditor: it reads every message in all
possible communication channels but does not modify, delay, inject, or drop them. It knows the protocol
and all of its public parameters, the tokenizer, the hash functions, and the session identifier, and it can run
any probabilistic polynomial-time computation. The auditor may also know the sender’s LLM and even its
internal state, i.e., the auditor knows the exact next token probability distribution of the sender’s outputs. In
the security definitions of Section 3.4 the auditor plays the role of the distinguisher, and we use the two terms
interchangeably.

3.5 Overview of CODETTA
CODETTA consists of a keyed steganographic protocol and a steganographic key exchange. The key exchange
runs first and establishes a shared secret key between the agents, and the keyed protocol then uses the
established key to transmit secret messages. Section 4 presents a strawman keyed construction with a fixed
alphabet and a model-free receiver, and proves the undetectability theorem that the later constructions inherit.
Section 5 builds the CODETTA keyed protocol, which uses a public draft model to raise the capacity of the
strawman under realistic multi-agent deployment of model and context asymmetry. Section 6 builds the key
exchange, and Section 7 evaluates CODETTA on three agent workloads.

6 CODETTA Steganographic Key Exchange
The protocols so far assume that the sender and the receiver share a key sk = (k
m
, k
v
). Independently deployed
agents have no such key, especially if they are hosted by different organizations. They cannot establish the
keys in the open, because a public key or a ciphertext in a conversation is an obvious signal to the auditor that
they are transmitting secrets. The key exchange itself must therefore be hidden in ordinary text without a key.
Hiding without a key is much more challenging than keyed scenarios. In the keyed protocols, the mask
is a pseudorandom pad that the auditor cannot compute without the key, while the sender and the receiver,
who both hold the key, compute the same pad and cancel it. The pad is uniform to the auditor, and Lemma 1
preserves the original distribution for every message. This construction does not generalize to the keyless
setting.
One keyless way to make a token carry a symbol is a public hash. The sender draws candidate blocks
of tokens from the base distribution and publishes one whose hash equals the symbol, and the receiver
recomputes the hash of the published block to read the symbol. Every party can compute the hash, so
every message is public. The transcript keeps the base distribution only if the symbols are uniform, because
otherwise the published blocks will be biased. A recent work follows this route [VZ26] and hides a key
exchange whose messages are pseudorandom, so that every symbol is uniform by construction. The cost
of this route lies in how the exchange is carried. The labels of a finite candidate pool are never perfectly
balanced, and a sender that keeps the transcript distribution exact has to publish a block with the wrong label
with probability equal to this imbalance, so a published symbol is wrong with a constant probability. The
key exchange of [VZ26] tolerates such noise at the level of key agreement, and the feedback compiler in its
Section 8 transmits the exchange bit by bit through a signaling protocol. Each published message carries a
single bit of a key-exchange message, and the sender publishes a fixed number of messages for every bit,
chosen in advance so that the receiver reads the bit correctly with high probability.
Section 7.4 estimates the cost of their construction on our workloads and compares it with CODETTA. The
same work also proves two impossibility results [VZ26]. First, a pseudorandom code whose decoder is public
cannot correct a constant fraction of bit flips; our carrier is not such a code, because the receiver decodes with
its MLWE secret and no public decoding information exists. Second, a non-interactive key exchange with a
pseudorandom transcript, in which the two messages are generated non-adaptively and every transcript bit is
flipped independently with a constant probability, admits a quasi-polynomial attack. Our exchange satisfies
neither condition. The sender’s response (w, z) depends on the share 
e

that it has read, so the messages are
adaptive, and the carrier only displaces each q-ary coefficient by a small amount, whereas the result assumes
that every transcript bit is flipped with a constant probability.

Ablations. To better understand the effectiveness of different components, we conduct three ablation studies.
First, we vary information asymmetry by revealing 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of the private context to
the receiver. Second, we vary model mismatch across same-model, cross-size, and cross-family sender–draft
pairs. Third, we remove one component of our code at a time by comparing with LDPC baselines: dropping
the draft model removes public channel estimation, and fixing the alphabet size removes adaptive alphabet
size selection, so the two variants separate the capacity gained from each.

sender model’s candidate pools under eight independent session identifiers, so Theorem 7 certifies the failure
probability under this measured displacement distribution. The carrier uses the first complete response block

7.2 Capacity of keyed protocols
Table 1 reports the payload rate of the three methods on the three workloads and the three model pairs. Every
cell recovered all 25 messages. CODETTA delivers between 4.1 and 6.4 times the rate of the draft-free LDPC
baseline and between 16 and 94 times the rate of ARS. The gain over the draft-free baseline is consistent
across models and workloads, and Section 7.3 separates the two components behind it. The absolute rates
differ by an order of magnitude across settings because they follow the entropy of the carrier text. Ministral
writes the most varied text and reaches 0.45 to 0.57 bits per token on FINANCIAL and IFEVAL. Qwen on
CTF is the other extreme. Its reports copy long spans of the private solve trajectory verbatim, 60% of the
body tokens have an entropy below 0.1 bits, and every method drops below 0.04 bits per token there.
Task quality. Theorem 3 guarantees that the covert transcripts follow the sender’s own distribution, so we do
not measure their perplexity and instead check the task quality directly on IFEVAL, whose scorer is automatic.
Ordinary responses of Qwen, Llama, and Ministral reach a strict instruction-following accuracy of 0.795,
0.795, and 0.744 on the evaluation prompts, and the covert transcripts of CODETTA reach 0.718, 0.795, and
0.615. No method differs significantly from ordinary generation under a two-sided exact McNemar test over
the 25 messages, with a smallest p-value of 0.125.
Speed. Embedding adds a draft forward pass and the coupling step to every token, and the throughput rows of
Table 1 present this cost. The CODETTA sender runs at 82% to 103% of the speed of the ARS sender across
the different models and tasks, and at 88% or higher in all but one, because generation time is dominated by
the base model and the draft is much smaller. The draft-free LDPC sender is the fastest, since it samples from
the base model with no draft at all.
For decoding cost, the two baselines decode with hashes alone and reach thousands to hundreds of
thousands of tokens per second, while the CODETTA receiver replays the draft model over the transcript and
decodes at 240 to 1,260 tokens per second, still 2 to 6 times faster than the sender generates.

7.3 Ablations of CODETTA keyed protocol
All ablations use the FINANCIAL workload and the Qwen2.5-7B sender.
Shared context. Figure 1 varies the fraction of the sender’s private records that the receiver also sees, from
the primary asymmetric setting, in which the receiver sees none of them, to identical prompts, in which the
receiver sees the whole record of 1,605 tokens on average. We plot two drafts, the 1.5B draft of the main
experiments and a 7B draft that is the same model as the sender. Capacity grows monotonically with the
shared context for both drafts: the 1.5B draft rises from 0.135 to 0.170 bits per token, and the 7B draft rises
from 0.132 to 0.231 bits per token. The gain comes from a draft that tracks the sender’s distribution more
closely, so that fewer proposals are rejected: the symbol error rate falls from 52% to 37% with the 1.5B draft
and from 43% to 17% with the 7B draft.
At full sharing with the 7B draft, the draft and base distributions coincide at every position, and the
remaining 17% comes from the bucket discretization alone. The figure also shows the value of a stronger
draft. Without shared context, the two drafts deliver the same capacity up to noise, since the 7B draft still has
to guess the private records. Once the receiver shares part of the context, the stronger draft delivers more, by
18% at half sharing and by 36% at full sharing. Accordingly, a stronger draft model yields a higher capacity
and its advantage grows with the shared portion of the sender’s context.
Model mismatch. Table 2 pairs each sender with drafts from all three families. Cross-family pairs use a
public byte-level bridge between the two tokenizers. In these experiments, the delivered payload rate varies
more across sender models than across draft models. Ministral keeps 0.32 to 0.45 bits per token with every
draft, and Qwen stays between 0.12 and 0.14. A same-family draft is best for each sender, and a cross-family
draft loses 8% to 29% against it.

Steganographic key exchange. Von Ahn and Hopper introduced public-key steganography and stegano-
graphic key exchange [VAH04]. As Vaikuntanathan and Zamir observe, the earlier covert key exchanges
assume covertexts that are generated non-adaptively and a min-entropy per message that grows with the
security parameter [VZ26]. Their own work is the closest to ours. With a shared key, they show that the tools
of undetectable watermarking and steganography give a covert conversation whose rate matches the entropy
of the honest messages up to constant factors. Without a key, they introduce pseudorandom noise-resilient key
exchange, prove that covert key exchange is possible when sufficiently many honest messages have constant
min-entropy, give constructions from sparse learning parity with noise and from a signaling compiler with
noiseless feedback, and prove that public pseudorandom codes cannot correct a constant fraction of bit flips
and that non-interactive protocols admit a quasi-polynomial attack. Section 6 compares the two key exchanges:
theirs is a feasibility result without an implementation, whereas CODETTA transports lattice coefficients
directly over the carrier, without a separate bitwise signaling layer, and certifies correctness empirically on
the measured channel, and Section 7.4 estimates the cost of their construction on our workloads.
Watermarking and speculative decoding. Undetectable and distortion-free watermarks sample each token
with randomness derived from a key so that the output distribution is unchanged, and their detectors need the
key but not the model [CGZ24, KTHL24, CG24]. A watermark carries a fixed signal instead of a message,
and the known limits of watermarking concern adversaries who edit or spoof the text [ZEF
+
24, PHZS24].
The maximal coupling of Section 4 is the acceptance rule of speculative decoding [LKM23, CBI
+
23], in
which a small draft model proposes tokens and the target model accepts or resamples them so that the output
keeps the target distribution exactly. CODETTA applies the same rule to a bucket-conditioned proposal and
treats a rejection as a channel error, while in speculative decoding, rejection reduces the decoding speedup.

model itself. Agents are prompted or trained to hide messages or reasoning in their text [MBS

+

content can change the model behaviors, so monitors and paraphrasers can detect or remove it. CODETTA is
instead a cryptographic protocol with a distribution-preservation guarantee of the output transcript, so the
passive auditors cannot observe the hidden collusion messages by inspecting the communication transcripts.
